namespace SimpleGraph
noncomputable def graphRamsey {α β : Type*} [Fintype α] [Fintype β]
    (G : SimpleGraph α) (H : SimpleGraph β) : ℕ :=
  sInf { n : ℕ | ∀ (C : SimpleGraph (Fin n)), G.IsContained C ∨ H.IsContained Cᶜ }
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
noncomputable def diagonalGraphRamsey {α : Type*} [Fintype α] (G : SimpleGraph α) : ℕ :=
  graphRamsey G G
end SimpleGraph

issues: B restricts to n ≥ 2 while A states no lower bound. For n = 1 the single-vertex tree has R(T) = 1 > 0 = 2n − 2, so the literal statement fails trivially there. The conjecture is intended for n ≥ 2, so this restriction is a benign correction, not a weakening.

The fallback convention R = 0 when no N exists never matters, because Ramsey numbers of finite graphs always exist. The property is monotone in N, so 'least N ≤ 2n−2' is equivalent to the property holding on K_{2n−2}, as B's restatement says.
Labeled vs unlabeled trees and non-induced copies both match the standard meaning of R(T) in A.
faithfulness.verdict: B is the standard statement of this conjecture for trees on n ≥ 2 vertices, the only range where it is meaningful, so a proof of B would settle A in the positive direction.
faithfulness.backtranslation:
For every integer n ≥ 2 and every tree T on n labeled vertices, the diagonal Ramsey number R(T, T) is at most 2n − 2. Here R(T, T) is the least natural number N with the following property: for every simple graph C on N vertices, either C contains a copy of T as a (not necessarily induced) subgraph, or the complement of C does. If no such N existed, the convention would set R(T, T) to 0.

Equivalently, in every red/blue coloring of the edges of the complete graph on 2n − 2 vertices, some color class contains a copy of T.
